title: What Counts as a Religion?
objective: After this level you can explain why scholars struggle to define religion, comparing a definition by belief in spiritual beings with one by what religion does for a community.
summary: Tylor defined religion by belief in spiritual beings; Durkheim by practices that unite a moral community. Each fits some traditions awkwardly, and in East Asia the word itself is new.

cards.headline: Try defining religion in one sentence. Scholars have argued since the 1870s.
cards.body: Every definition seems to leave someone out, or let too much in. Here are the two classic attempts, and why the problem runs deeper than wording.

cards.headline: Definition one: what people believe
cards.body: In 1871 the anthropologist Edward Tylor offered a minimum definition: religion is belief in spiritual beings. Scholars call this kind of definition substantive, because it names the content: spirits, gods or other unseen realities. It's short and tidy. But definitions built on belief in gods fit some traditions awkwardly. Buddhist teaching, for example, does not center on a creator God, yet scholars widely count Buddhism as a religion.

cards.headline: Definition two: what religion does
cards.body: In 1912 the sociologist Emile Durkheim took the other road. For him a religion is a unified system of beliefs and practices about sacred things, things "set apart and forbidden", which unite everyone who shares them into one moral community. The weight falls on the second half. Scholars call this a functional definition: religion is known by the role it plays, like binding people together. It needs no gods at all, which is exactly why some find it too roomy.

cards.headline: Even the word is local
cards.body: The trouble runs deeper than wording. The concept of religion reached East Asia with scholars only about a century ago, and everyday translations, like Chinese zongjiao, often suggest organized, hierarchical religions rather than traditional practice. In late imperial China a devoted Confucian scholar could join Daoist or Buddhist rituals with no sense of switching sides. Try sorting that into one box. The box, not the people, is what doesn't fit.

cards.headline: What Counts as a Religion?: the takeaways
learned: Tylor defined religion as belief in spiritual beings
Durkheim defined it by a community united around sacred things
Every definition fits some traditions awkwardly

questions.prompt: Match each name with the idea it goes with.
questions.explanation: Tylor defined religion as belief in spiritual beings. Durkheim said religion unites people into one moral community. Chinese zongjiao often suggests organized, hierarchical religions.

questions.prompt: Durkheim's definition is called functional. What does that mean?

options.label: It depends on belief in a creator God above all else
options.rationale: That would be a definition by content.

options.label: It counts only religions with scriptures
It measures how many people attend services
It judges religion by what it does, like uniting people

questions.explanation: A functional definition looks at what religion does: for Durkheim, uniting people into one moral community.

questions.prompt: Why is it tricky to apply the word 'religion' to traditional practice in China?

options.label: Chinese people have never had rituals or sacred places of any kind
options.rationale: Rituals there are rich and old.

options.label: The concept arrived only about a century ago and suggests organized churches
Chinese law has always banned the word
options.rationale: The problem is meaning, not law.

options.label: Confucian scholars refused to take part in rituals
options.rationale: They could join Daoist and Buddhist rituals.

questions.explanation: 'Religion' reached East Asia with scholars about a century ago, and translations like zongjiao suggest organized religions, while people often combined traditions.
